terraform-kubernetes.wrapped_text:
Terraform for Kubernetes
Kubernetes is a system that runs
containers on a group of machines,
called a cluster. You describe
objects, such as a Deployment that
runs copies of a container or a
Service that gives them one
address, and the cluster keeps the
real state equal to the
description. On AWS, Amazon EKS
(Elastic Kubernetes Service) runs
the cluster's control plane for
you. The [Terraform
map](../terraform.md) explains
Terraform itself.

Terraform reaches a cluster on EKS
through four providers:

- `hashicorp/aws` builds the
cluster itself: the control plane,
the node groups, add-ons and
access rules.
- `hashicorp/kubernetes` creates
Kubernetes objects inside the
cluster, one typed resource per
kind, plus `kubernetes_manifest`
for any kind ([provider docs](http
s://registry.terraform.io/provider
s/hashicorp/kubernetes/latest/docs
)).
- `hashicorp/helm` installs Helm
charts. A chart is a package of
Kubernetes objects with settings,
called values; one installed chart
is a release ([provider docs](http
s://registry.terraform.io/provider
s/hashicorp/helm/latest/docs)).
- A community `kubectl` provider
applies raw YAML files, as the
`kubectl apply` command does.

The unit is one cluster. The last
three providers need the cluster's
address, its certificate and a
short-lived token. They get them
from the cluster that the first
provider built, which creates the
central problem of this setup
([Two APIs, One Depends on the Oth
er](#two-apis-one-depends-on-the-o
ther-two-apis-one-depends-on-the-o
ther)).

Five more ideas explain most
plans:

- Three records describe each
release: the Terraform state,
Helm's own record, and the live
objects ([Three Records of Truth](
#three-records-of-truth-three-reco
rds-of-truth)).
- Each field of a live object has
one owner: Terraform, Helm, a
controller or EKS ([Every Field
Has One Owner](#every-field-has-on
e-owner-every-field-has-one-owner)
).
- Custom resource definitions
(CRDs) add new kinds to a cluster,
and they have their own lifecycle
([CRDs Have Their Own Lifecycle](#
crds-have-their-own-lifecycle-crds
-have-their-own-lifecycle)).
- A finished apply does not mean a
healthy cluster ([Apply Complete
Is Not Healthy](#apply-complete-is
-not-healthy-apply-complete-is-not
-healthy)).
- Identity crosses between AWS and
Kubernetes in two directions ([Two
Identity Bridges](#two-identity-br
idges-two-identity-bridges)).

Now compare Snowflake. Snowflake
runs a statement once, and the
object stays as created.
Kubernetes runs control loops that
keep changing objects towards
their description, and some
controllers add fields of their
own. So in Kubernetes, more of
what a plan shows depends on who
else acted after the last apply.

The map has four parts. Mental
Models explains the ideas above.
Reading a Kubernetes Configuration
says what you will see and where
to look first. Pitfalls lists the
failures that experienced users
plan around. Good and Bad
Decisions compares the common
design choices.
terraform-kubernetes.wrapped_original_text:
Terraform for Kubernetes
Kubernetes is a system that runs containers on a group of machines, called a cluster. You describe objects, such as a Deployment that runs copies of a container or a Service that gives them one address, and the cluster keeps the real state equal to the description. On AWS, Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) runs the cluster's control plane for you. The [Terraform map](../terraform.md) explains Terraform itself.

Terraform reaches a cluster on EKS through four providers:

- `hashicorp/aws` builds the cluster itself: the control plane, the node groups, add-ons and access rules.
- `hashicorp/kubernetes` creates Kubernetes objects inside the cluster, one typed resource per kind, plus `kubernetes_manifest` for any kind ([provider docs](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/kubernetes/latest/docs)).
- `hashicorp/helm` installs Helm charts. A chart is a package of Kubernetes objects with settings, called values; one installed chart is a release ([provider docs](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/helm/latest/docs)).
- A community `kubectl` provider applies raw YAML files, as the `kubectl apply` command does.

The unit is one cluster. The last three providers need the cluster's address, its certificate and a short-lived token. They get them from the cluster that the first provider built, which creates the central problem of this setup ([Two APIs, One Depends on the Other](#two-apis-one-depends-on-the-other-two-apis-one-depends-on-the-other)).

Five more ideas explain most plans:

- Three records describe each release: the Terraform state, Helm's own record, and the live objects ([Three Records of Truth](#three-records-of-truth-three-records-of-truth)).
- Each field of a live object has one owner: Terraform, Helm, a controller or EKS ([Every Field Has One Owner](#every-field-has-one-owner-every-field-has-one-owner)).
- Custom resource definitions (CRDs) add new kinds to a cluster, and they have their own lifecycle ([CRDs Have Their Own Lifecycle](#crds-have-their-own-lifecycle-crds-have-their-own-lifecycle)).
- A finished apply does not mean a healthy cluster ([Apply Complete Is Not Healthy](#apply-complete-is-not-healthy-apply-complete-is-not-healthy)).
- Identity crosses between AWS and Kubernetes in two directions ([Two Identity Bridges](#two-identity-bridges-two-identity-bridges)).

Now compare Snowflake. Snowflake runs a statement once, and the object stays as created. Kubernetes runs control loops that keep changing objects towards their description, and some controllers add fields of their own. So in Kubernetes, more of what a plan shows depends on who else acted after the last apply.

The map has four parts. Mental Models explains the ideas above. Reading a Kubernetes Configuration says what you will see and where to look first. Pitfalls lists the failures that experienced users plan around. Good and Bad Decisions compares the common design choices.

two-apis-one-depends-on-the-other.wrapped_text:
Two APIs, One Depends on the Other
Terraform builds the cluster through the AWS
API. Then it talks to the Kubernetes API with
credentials that come from that same cluster.
The Kubernetes provider warns that the cluster
and the Kubernetes resources should not be
created in the same module. Its docs call
separate applies "the most reliable way"
([provider docs](https://github.com/hashicorp/
terraform-provider-kubernetes/blob/v3.5.0/docs
/index.md#L42-L44)). Its EKS example therefore
uses two folders: one for the cluster and one
for what runs inside ([EKS example](https://gi
thub.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-kubernet
es/blob/v3.5.0/_examples/eks/README.md)).

An EKS token is short-lived: AWS signs it for
15 minutes, and the AWS command-line tool
marks it as expired after 14 ([get-token code]
(https://github.com/aws/aws-cli/blob/2.42.1/aw
scli/customizations/eks/get_token.py#L132-L136
)). An `exec` block in the provider settings
runs `aws eks get-token` for a fresh token on
every run ([exec plugins](https://github.com/h
ashicorp/terraform-provider-kubernetes/blob/v3
.5.0/docs/index.md#L108-L124)). So the machine
that runs Terraform needs the AWS command-line
tool.

three-records-of-truth.wrapped_text:
Three Records of Truth
A `helm_release` leaves three records:

1. The Terraform state holds the inputs: the
chart, its version and its values.
2. Helm keeps its own record of each release,
with the rendered objects, in a Secret in the
cluster.
3. The live objects run in the cluster.

A `helm upgrade` or a `kubectl edit` outside
Terraform changes the second or the third
record, but not the first. So the plan can say
"No changes" while the cluster differs from
the code ([issue 372](https://github.com/hashi
corp/terraform-provider-helm/issues/372)). The
helm provider has an option that stores the
rendered objects in the state, so a plan can
compare them ([manifest experiment](https://gi
thub.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-helm/blo
b/v3.3.0/docs/index.md#L201-L213)).

every-field-has-one-owner.wrapped_text:
Every Field Has One Owner
Kubernetes records which client set each field
of an object. With server-side apply, it
reports a conflict when a second client tries
to set the same field ([server-side apply](htt
ps://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/se
rver-side-apply/)). Controllers also set
fields after Terraform creates an object. For
example, the AWS Load Balancer Controller sets
the class of a Service that asks for a load
balancer. A diff that comes back after every
apply means two owners write one field.

crds-have-their-own-lifecycle.wrapped_text:
CRDs Have Their Own Lifecycle
A custom resource definition adds a new kind
to the cluster's API, such as `PrometheusRule`
or `ExternalSecret`. Charts often bring their
CRDs in a `crds` folder. Helm installs that
folder once and never upgrades or deletes it:
"There is no support at this time for
upgrading or deleting CRDs using Helm" ([Helm
CRD guide](https://github.com/helm/helm-www/bl
ob/d869ccd3db838b63cee08bffb8400e1a9221c3ee/ve
rsioned_docs/version-3/chart_best_practices/cu
stom_resource_definitions.md#L30-L45)). A
custom resource, an object of such a kind, can
only exist after its CRD exists. That creates
an order between charts, and between charts
and the resources that use their kinds.

apply-complete-is-not-healthy.wrapped_text:
Apply Complete Is Not Healthy
Terraform reports success when the API accepts
the objects. Whether the pods then run depends
on images, resources and configuration.
`helm_release` waits for its objects by
default, for up to 300 seconds per operation
([release doc](https://github.com/hashicorp/te
rraform-provider-helm/blob/v3.3.0/docs/resourc
es/release.md#L59-L64)). Setting `wait =
false` makes applies faster, but then a broken
release also reports success. The
`kubectl_manifest` resource waits only for a
Deployment to roll out ([kubectl doc](https://
github.com/gavinbunney/terraform-provider-kube
ctl/blob/v1.19.0/docs/resources/kubectl_manife
st.md#L37)).

two-identity-bridges.wrapped_text:
Two Identity Bridges
Identity crosses between AWS and Kubernetes in
two directions:

- From AWS into Kubernetes: an IAM principal
becomes a Kubernetes user. EKS does this with
access entries, managed through the AWS API,
or with the older `aws-auth` ConfigMap inside
the cluster ([access to clusters](https://docs
.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/grant-k8s
-access.html)).
- From a pod out to AWS: a pod gets an IAM
role. EKS does this with IAM roles for service
accounts (IRSA), or with EKS Pod Identity
([pod identities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/
eks/latest/userguide/pod-identities.html)).

Access entries are managed only through the
AWS provider, so granting access needs no
working connection to the cluster.

k8s-what-you-will-see.wrapped_text:
What You Will See
| Resource | What it is | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `aws_eks_cluster` | the control plane |
Kubernetes version, access mode, endpoint
access |
| `aws_eks_node_group` | a group of worker
machines | Machine image source, sizes,
ignored fields |
| `aws_eks_addon` | an EKS add-on, such as the
network plugin | Pinned version per Kubernetes
version |
| `aws_eks_access_entry` | IAM principal
mapped to Kubernetes access | Who gets cluster
admin |
| `helm_release` | one installed chart |
`version`, values source, `wait`, `atomic`,
`timeout` |
| `kubernetes_deployment`,
`kubernetes_config_map`, and other typed
resources | one object of a known kind |
Namespace, labels, restarts on config change |
| `kubernetes_manifest` | any object,
including custom resources | The CRD it needs
at plan time |
| `kubectl_manifest` | raw YAML, from a
community provider | Which fork, and
server-side apply |
| `kubernetes_secret` | a Secret | Its data
sits in the state in plain text |

A chart can also be configured from a template
file with `templatefile`, which renders the
values from variables. The rendered values
then appear in the plan as one block of text.

k8s-where-to-look-first.wrapped_text:
Where to Look First
Read a Kubernetes configuration in this order:

1. `required_providers`, the lock file and the
Terraform version pin. The helm provider
changed its syntax in version 3, so the
version tells you which docs apply ([v3
upgrade guide](https://github.com/hashicorp/te
rraform-provider-helm/blob/v3.3.0/docs/guides/
v3-upgrade-guide.md)).
2. The `provider "kubernetes"` and `provider
"helm"` blocks. Find where the host,
certificate and token come from. If the
cluster is built in the same configuration,
look for a documented bootstrap order.
3. The backend and how environments switch:
workspaces, variable files or backend
settings.
4. The pipeline: plan and apply, saved plan or
not, approvals, `-target` steps and secret
injection.
5. The cluster definition: version, access
mode, access entries, add-on pins, endpoint
access and node groups.
6. Each `helm_release`: the version pin,
`wait`, `atomic`, `timeout`, CRD handling and
secrets in values.
7. Each custom resource: which CRD it needs,
which chart installs that CRD, and which
resource type applies it.
8. The secret paths: `kubernetes_secret`, Helm
values, and an operator that reads a secret
store.
9. The `lifecycle` blocks, `ignore_changes`,
and checksum annotations. Each one marks a
problem someone already met.

Plan Signals
| Line in the plan | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Errors such as `Failed to construct REST
client` on every Kubernetes resource | The
provider settings depend on a cluster that the
plan will create or replace. |
| `no matches for kind "PrometheusRule"` | A

installed yet. |
| `metadata` of a `helm_release` as `(known

. |
| `-/+` on a Service of type LoadBalancer in
every apply | A controller set a field that
cannot change; the load balancer gets a new
address each time. |
| `(sensitive value)` in place of all Helm
values | One sensitive input made the whole
values text sensitive. |

providers-from-same-apply.wrapped_text:
Providers from the Same Apply
When the provider settings read the cluster's
address from resources in the same
configuration, a plan for a new or replaced
cluster has no address yet. Every Kubernetes
resource then fails, for example with "Failed
to construct REST client" ([issue 1775](https:
//github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-kube
rnetes/issues/1775)), or calls `localhost`.
Separate states for the cluster and for what
runs inside it fix this. A documented
bootstrap with `-target` works too, but
Terraform reserves `-target` for exceptional
cases ([plan command](https://developer.hashic
orp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan)).

CRDs Needed at Plan Time
`kubernetes_manifest` reads the API schema of
its kind during the plan, so the cluster must
be reachable and the CRD must exist ([manifest
doc](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-pr
ovider-kubernetes/blob/v3.5.0/docs/resources/m
anifest.md#L82)). A custom resource planned in
the same run as the chart that installs its
CRD fails with `no matches for kind`. Three
ways out: install the CRDs in an earlier
apply; use `kubectl_manifest`, which looks up
the kind only at apply time ([kubectl code](ht
tps://github.com/gavinbunney/terraform-provide
r-kubectl/blob/v1.19.0/kubernetes/resource_kub
ectl_manifest.go#L218-L245)); or put the
custom resources into a small chart of their
own.

helm-does-not-upgrade-crds.wrapped_text:
Helm Does Not Upgrade CRDs
A chart upgrade that brings new CRD versions
in its `crds` folder installs the new chart,
but the old CRDs stay. New fields of the
custom resources then fail. The plan shows
only a new `version`. Each chart documents its
own way to upgrade CRDs, for example with
`kubectl apply` of the chart's CRD files.
Charts that render their CRDs as normal
templates do upgrade them, but they can also
delete them when the release is removed, which
deletes every custom resource of that kind.
helm-does-not-upgrade-crds.wrapped_original_text:
Helm Does Not Upgrade CRDs
A chart upgrade that brings new CRD versions in its `crds` folder installs the new chart, but the old CRDs stay. New fields of the custom resources then fail. The plan shows only a new `version`. Each chart documents its own way to upgrade CRDs, for example with `kubectl apply` of the chart's CRD files. Charts that render their CRDs as normal templates do upgrade them, but they can also delete them when the release is removed, which deletes every custom resource of that kind.

failed-and-stuck-releases.wrapped_text:
Failed and Stuck Releases
When an install fails, the release can stay in
Helm's record. The next apply then fails with
"cannot re-use a name that is still in use"
([issue 1886](https://github.com/hashicorp/ter
raform-provider-helm/issues/1886)). An apply
that is killed mid-operation can leave the
release in a `pending-*` state, and every
later run fails with "another operation
(install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress".
Recovery needs `helm rollback` or `helm
uninstall` by hand. `atomic = true` removes a
failed install automatically; it defaults to
`false` ([release doc](https://github.com/hash
icorp/terraform-provider-helm/blob/v3.3.0/docs
/resources/release.md#L25)).

secrets-in-helm-values.wrapped_text:
Secrets in Helm Values
Helm values are part of the release resource.
A secret written into `values`, for example a
webhook URL, can print in clear text in a plan
when the release changes or is destroyed; only
values passed through `set_sensitive` stay
hidden ([issue 1287](https://github.com/hashic
orp/terraform-provider-helm/issues/1287)). The
opposite problem also happens: when a values
template reads one sensitive variable, the
whole values text becomes sensitive, and
reviewers see no diff at all. Pass secrets
through `set_sensitive` or the write-only
`set_wo`, or let an operator read them from a
secret store at run time.

invisible-drift.wrapped_text:
Invisible Drift
A chart that someone upgraded by hand, an
object that someone edited, or an image tag
`latest` that moved: none of these shows in a
plan, because Terraform compares only its
inputs (see Three Records of Truth). Pin chart
versions and image tags, and do not change
Terraform-managed releases by hand.

controller-fields-force-replacement.wrapped_text:
Controller Fields Force Replacement
The AWS Load Balancer Controller sets
`spec.loadBalancerClass` when a Service of
type LoadBalancer is created ([controller docs
](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-load-
balancer-controller/blob/v3.6.3/docs/deploy/in
stallation.md#L12-L13)). That field cannot
change, and the Kubernetes provider replaces
the Service when it differs from the code. So
every apply deletes and recreates the Service,
and the load balancer gets a new address.
Write the field into the configuration with
the value that the controller sets.

k8s-secrets-in-state.wrapped_text:
Secrets in State
The data of a `kubernetes_secret` sits in the
state in plain text ([secret doc](https://gith
ub.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-kubernetes
/blob/v3.5.0/docs/resources/secret_v1.md#L14))
. The write-only argument `data_wo` keeps it
out, with Terraform 1.11 or later. An operator
that copies secrets from AWS Secrets Manager
into the cluster keeps them out of Terraform
entirely.

access-through-aws-auth.wrapped_text:
Access Through aws-auth
The `aws-auth` ConfigMap holds all
IAM-to-Kubernetes mappings in one object,
including the entries that let nodes join the
cluster. A configuration that writes the whole
object must keep those entries, or nodes lose
access. EKS access entries replace the
ConfigMap. The access mode moves one way only:
from `CONFIG_MAP` to `API_AND_CONFIG_MAP` to
`API` ([EKS module upgrade notes](https://gith
ub.com/terraform-aws-modules/terraform-aws-eks
/blob/v21.30.2/docs/UPGRADE-20.0.md#L221-L223)
). Keep the node entries that EKS created
until matching access entries exist
([migrating to access entries](https://docs.aw
s.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/migrating-ac
cess-entries.html)).

k8s-version-upgrades.wrapped_text:
Version Upgrades
EKS raises the control plane one minor version
per update, and the nodes must catch up before
the next step ([update a cluster](https://docs
.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/update-cl
uster.html)). Add-on versions belong to a
Kubernetes version, so each version change
also changes add-on pins. A node group that
reads its machine image version from AWS's
"recommended" parameter replaces its nodes
whenever AWS publishes a new image, even
during an unrelated change ([node group doc](h
ttps://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider
-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/r/eks_node_grou
p.html.markdown#L69-L77)). A node replacement
drains pods, and it fails after 15 minutes if
pods cannot be evicted ([node updates](https:/
/docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/mana
ged-node-update-behavior.html)).

Add-on versions belong to a Kubernetes version, so each version change also changes add-on pins. A node group that reads its machine image version from AWS's "recommended" parameter replaces its nodes whenever AWS publishes a new image, even during an unrelated change ([node group doc](https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-aws/blob/v6.73.0/website/docs/r/eks_node_group.html.markdown#L69-L77)). A node replacement drains pods, and it fails after 15 minutes if pods cannot be evicted ([node updates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/managed-node-update-behavior.html)).

networkpolicies-need-an-enforcer.wrapped_text:
NetworkPolicies Need an Enforcer
A NetworkPolicy object has no effect unless
the cluster's network plugin enforces it
([network policies](https://kubernetes.io/docs
/concepts/services-networking/network-policies
/)). On EKS, the VPC CNI plugin enforces
policies only when its `enableNetworkPolicy`
setting is on ([configure network policy](http
s://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/userguide/c
ni-network-policy-configure.html)). Without
it, Terraform creates the policies, the plan
is clean, and all traffic still flows.

split-the-cluster.wrapped_text:
Split the Cluster from Its Contents
The Kubernetes provider recommends separate
applies for the cluster and for what runs
inside it. Two states give reliable plans even
when the cluster is new or replaced, at the
cost of two pipelines and a data source that
connects them. One state gives one plan per
change, at the cost of a manual bootstrap with
`-target` steps.

fresh-tokens-with-exec.wrapped_text:
Fresh Tokens with exec
An `exec` block fetches a new token for each
run, so a long apply does not fail when a
token expires, and no token lands in the
state. The provider docs forbid mixing `exec`
with other credential settings ([exec plugins]
(https://github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provid
er-kubernetes/blob/v3.5.0/docs/index.md#L112))
. The cost is the AWS command-line tool on
every runner.

pin-every-version-axis.wrapped_text:
Pin Every Version Axis
A cluster has many versions that move on their
own: the control plane, the node image, the
add-ons, the charts, the CRDs, the container
images and the providers. Without `version`,
`helm_release` installs the latest chart
([release doc](https://github.com/hashicorp/te
rraform-provider-helm/blob/v3.3.0/docs/resourc
es/release.md#L63)). Pin each axis, commit the
lock file, and raise each pin in its own
reviewed change.

Atomic Releases with Real Timeouts
`atomic = true` with a realistic `timeout`
rolls a failed install back and reports the
failure. `wait = false` makes applies shorter,
but it reports broken releases as successes.
Prefer the first for anything that other
systems depend on.
